EXPOSÉ II
Report on the trace formula

In this text, I have tried to present as directly as possible Grothendieck's cohomological theory of \(L\)-functions. I follow very closely some of the talks given by Grothendieck at the IHES in the spring of 1966. In the spirit of this volume, no appeal will be made to SGA 5 – except for two references to passages of Exposé XI, which is independent of the rest of that seminar.
In §10 (pp. 81-90) of [13], the reader will find a summary of the theory, in the crucial case of curves.
1 Some reminders
1.1 Notations

\(p,q,\mathbb{F},\mathbb{F}_q\): \(p\) is a prime number, \(q=p^f\) a power of \(p\), and \(\mathbb{F}\) an algebraic closure of the prime field \(\mathbb{F}_p\). For every power \(p^n\) of \(p\), we denote by \(\mathbb{F}_{p^n}\) the subfield of \(\mathbb{F}\) with \(p^n\) elements.

\(X_0,X\): We shall often denote an object over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) by a symbol carrying an index \(0\). The same symbol, without the \(0\), then denotes the object deduced from it by extension of scalars to \(\mathbb{F}\). For example, if \(\mathscr{F}_0\) is a sheaf on a scheme \(X_0\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), we denote by \(\mathscr{F}\) its inverse image on \(X=X_0\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q} \mathbb{F}\).

\(F\): If \(X_0\) is a scheme over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), we call Frobenius morphism, and denote by \(F\), the endomorphism of \(X_0\) that “sends the point with coordinates \(x\) to the one with coordinates \(x^q\)”: it is the identity on the underlying topological space and, for \(x\) a local section of the structure sheaf, \(F^* x = x^q\).

We again denote by \(F\) the endomorphism of \(X\) deduced from it by extension of scalars. On the set \(X(\mathbb{F}) = X_0(\mathbb{F})\) of rational points of \(X\), \(F\) acts as the Frobenius substitution \(\varphi\in\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}/\mathbb{F}_q)\) defined by \(\varphi(x)=x^q\). In particular, \(X^F=X_0(\mathbb{F}_q)\).
In case of ambiguity, we shall write \(F_{(q)}\) rather than \(F\).
1.2 Frobenius correspondence
Let \(X_0\) be a scheme over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and \(\mathscr{F}_0\) a sheaf on \(X_0\). I like to view the Frobenius correspondence (an \(F\)-endomorphism of \(\mathscr{F}_0\)) as follows:
\[ \tag{1.2.1} F^* : F^*\mathscr{F}_0 \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathscr{F}_0 \]

We regard \(\mathscr{F}_0\) as the sheaf of local sections of a space \([\mathscr{F}_0]\) étale over \(X_0\) (\([\mathscr{F}_0]\) is an algebraic space in the sense of M. Artin). The functoriality of \(F\) yields a commutative diagram
\[ \xymatrix{ [\mathscr{F}_0] \ar[r]^-F \ar[d] & [\mathscr{F}_0] \ar[d] \\ X_0 \ar[r]^F & X_0 } \]

Because \([\mathscr{F}_0]\) is étale over \(X_0\), this diagram is cartesian; it yields an isomorphism \([\mathscr{F}_0]\xrightarrow{\sim} F^*[\mathscr{F}_0]\) with inverse (1.2.1). We again denote by \(F^*\) the correspondences or morphisms deduced from \(F\) by extension of scalars or by functoriality, such as \(F^*:\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X,\mathscr{F})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X,\mathscr{F})\).
For a formal definition, I refer to [21]. Only the case \(q=p\) is considered there, but the general case is treated in the same way.

The Frobenius correspondence is functorial in \((X_0,\mathscr{F}_0)\). If \(f_0:X_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y_0\) is a morphism of \(\mathbb{F}_q\)-schemes, \(\mathscr{F}_0\) a sheaf on \(X_0\), \(\mathscr{G}_0\) a sheaf on \(Y_0\), and \(u\in\hom(f_0^*\mathscr{G}_0,\mathscr{F}_0)\) an \(f_0\)-morphism from \(\mathscr{G}_0\) to \(\mathscr{F}_0\), then we have a commutative diagram of spaces \(f_0 F = F f_0\), and above it a commutative diagram of sheaves

\[ \xymatrix{ X_0 \ar[r]^-{f_0} \ar[d]^-F & Y_0 \ar[d]^-F \\ X_0 \ar[r]^-{f_0} & Y_0 }\qquad\qquad \xymatrix{ \mathscr{F}_0 & \mathscr{G}_0 \ar[l]_-u\\ \mathscr{F}_0 \ar[u]_-{F^*} & \mathscr{G}_0 \ar[u]^-{F^*} \ar[l]} \]
In particular, the correspondence on \(f_{0*}\mathscr{F}_0\) deduced from the Frobenius correspondence of \((X_0,\mathscr{F}_0)\) is the Frobenius correspondence of \((U_0,f_{0*}\mathscr{F}_0)\).

The natural morphism \(Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y_0\) is a limit of étale morphisms. It follows that for every abelian sheaf \(\mathscr{F}_0\) on \(X_0\), the inverse images on \(Y\) of the \(\mathsf{R}^if_0\mathscr{F}_0\) are the \(\mathsf{R}^if_*\mathscr{F}\).
On \(\mathsf{R}^if_*\mathscr{F}\), we have

1. the correspondence \(F^*\mathsf{R}^i f_*\mathscr{F} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R}^i f_*\mathscr{F} \xrightarrow{F^*} \mathsf{R}^if_*\mathscr{F}\) deduced by functoriality from the Frobenius correspondence;

  2. the correspondence \(F^*\mathsf{R}^if_*\mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathsf{R}^if_*\mathscr{F}\), the inverse image on \(Y\) of the Frobenius correspondence on \(\mathsf{R}^ii f_{0*}\mathscr{F}_0\).
We deduce from (1.3) that these correspondences coincide. They induce the initial term of an action of Frobenius on the whole spectral sequence
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(Y,\mathsf{R}^q f_*\mathscr{F}) \rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{p+q}(X,\mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]
Likewise in cohomology with proper support, and for the spectral sequence
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^p(Y,\mathsf{R}^q f_* \mathscr{F}) \rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^{p+q}(X,\mathscr{F}) \]
1.5 Change of finite field

Let \((X_0,\mathscr{F}_0)\) be over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), \(n\) an integer, and \((X_1,\mathscr{F}_1)\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\) deduced from \((X_0,\mathscr{F}_0)\) by extension of scalars. On the one hand we have the Frobenius correspondence \(F_{(q)}:X_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_0)\), \(F_{(q)}^*:F_{(q)}^*\mathscr{F}_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{F}_0\), and on the other hand \(F_{(q^n)}:X_1\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X_1\), \(F_{(q^n)}^*:F_{(q^n)}^*\mathscr{F}_1\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{F}_1\). One checks easily that \(F_{(q^n)}\) is deduced from the \(n\)-th power of \(F_{(q)}\) by extension of scalars from \(\mathbb{F}_q\) to \(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\); after extension of scalars to \(\mathbb{F}\), one still has the same identity \(F_{(q^n)}=F_{(q)}^n\) between endomorphisms of \(X\) and correspondences on \(X\).

If \(x\) is a closed point of \(X_0\), with \([k(x),\mathbb{F}_q]=n\), and \(\overline{x}\in X_0(\mathbb{F}) = X(\mathbb{F})\) lies over \(x\), then \(\overline{x}\) is a fixed point of \(F_{(q^n)}=F_{(q)}^n\). We denote by \(F_x^*\) the endomorphism of \(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{x}}\) induced by \(F_{(q^n)}^*\). Up to isomorphism, \((F_{\overline{x}}^*,\mathscr{F}_{\overline{x}})\) does not depend on the choice of \(\overline{x}\). The trace, etc. of \(F_x^*\) is denoted by a notation such as \(\operatorname{tr}(F_x^*,\mathscr{F})\).
1.6 \(L\)-function

Let \(X_0\) be a scheme of finite type over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). We denote by \(|X_0|\) the set of its closed points and, for \(x\in |X_0|\), we set \(\deg(x)=[k(x),\mathbb{F}_p]\). If \(\mathscr{F}_0\) is a \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaf on \(X_0\) (for this notion, see below) – or a constructible flat sheaf of modules over a commutative noetherian ring \(A\), we denote by \(L(X_0,\mathscr{F}_0)\) the formal power series with constant term \(1\), in \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell[\![ t]\!]\) or in \(A[\![ t]\!]\),
\[ L(X_0,\mathscr{F}_0) = \prod_{x\in|X_0|} \det\left(1-F_x^* t^{\deg(x)},\mathscr{F}\right)^{-1} \text{.} \]
1.7 Remark

In the definition (1.6), one has \(\deg(x)=[k(x),\mathbb{F}_p]\) (absolute degree) and not \(\deg(x)=[k(x),\mathbb{F}_q]\) (degree relative to \(\mathbb{F}_q\)). This has the effect that \(L(X_0,\mathscr{F}_0)\) depends only on the scheme \(X_0\) and the sheaf \(\mathscr{F}_0\), not on \(q\) and the structure morphism \(X_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{F}_q)\). The indeterminate \(t\) is an avatar of \(p^{-s}\).
1.8 The Galois point of view

This n\(^\circ\) will not be used in the rest of the report. For \(\mathscr{F}_0\) an abelian sheaf on \(X_0\), the Galois group \(\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}/\mathbb{F}_q)\) acts on \(\mathbb{F}\), and by transport of structure on \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\). In particular, the Frobenius substitution \(\varphi\) (1.1) induces an automorphism, again denoted \(\varphi\), of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\). The Frobenius correspondence, for its part, defines an endomorphism \(F^*\) of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\). We have
\[ \tag{1.8.1} {F^*}^{-1} = \varphi \qquad \text{(on } \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \text{).} \]

To see this, let us apply (1.4) to the case where \(Y_0\) is a point: \(Y_0=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{F}_q)\). One finds that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\) is the fibre, at the geometric point \(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{F})\) of \(Y_0\), of \(\mathsf{R}^i f_! \mathscr{F}_0\), and that \(F^*\) is the fibre of the Frobenius correspondence of \(\mathsf{R}^i f_!\mathscr{F}_0\). Let \([\mathsf{R}^i f_! \mathscr{F}_0]\) be as in (1.2). One has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F}) = [\mathsf{R}^i f_!\mathscr{F}_0](\mathbb{F})\) and

1. \(\varphi\) acts by transport of structure, via its action on \(\mathbb{F}\),

  2. \(F^*\) is the inverse of \(F:[\mathsf{R}^i f_!\mathscr{F}_0](\mathbb{F}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} [\mathsf{R}^i f_!\mathscr{F}_0](\mathbb{F})\).
We conclude by the identity \(F=\varphi\) of (1.1).
One of the merits of the Galois point of view is that it allows one to reason by transport of structure.
2 \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaves
The notion of \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaf is developed in detail in [21]. We shall use only the definitions and results below.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.1

Let \(X\) be a noetherian scheme. A \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) on \(X\) is a projective system of sheaves \(\mathscr{F}_n\) (\(n\geqslant 0\)), with \(\mathscr{F}_n\) a sheaf of constructible \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1}\)-modules [2], and such that the transition morphism \(\mathscr{F}_n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{F}_{n-1}\) factors through an isomorphism

\[ \mathscr{F}_n\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1}} \mathbb{Z}/\ell^n \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathscr{F}_{n-1}\text{.} \]

We say that \(\mathscr{F}\) is smooth if the \(\mathscr{F}_n\) are locally constant.
The terminology of [21] is different: there one says “constructible \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf” for “\(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf,” and “constructible twisted constant” for “smooth.”
Likewise, below, for \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaves.

If \(k\) is a separably closed field, a sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)-modules on \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\) is identified with a \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)-module, and the functor \(\mathscr{F}\mapsto \varprojlim \mathscr{F}_n\) identifies the \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaves on \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\) with the \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-modules of finite type. This justifies the following definition: the fibre of the \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) at the geometric point \(x\) of \(X\) is the \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-module \(\varprojlim (\mathscr{F}_n)_x\).

Suppose \(X\) is connected, and let \(x\) be a geometric point of \(X\). It is known that the functor “fibre at \(x\)” is an equivalence of the category of locally constant constructible sheaves of \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)-modules with the category of \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)-modules of finite type equipped with a continuous action of \(\pi_1(X,x)\). By passage to the limit, one deduces the following proposition.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.4

Under the above hypotheses, the functor “fibre at \(x\)” is an equivalence of the category of smooth \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaves on \(X\) with that of \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-modules of finite type equipped with a continuous action of \(\pi_1(X,x)\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.5

Let \(\mathscr{F}\) be a \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf on a noetherian scheme \(X\). There exists a finite partition of \(X\) into locally closed subsets \(X_i\) such that the \(\mathscr{F}|X_i\) are smooth.

Set \(\operatorname{gr}_\ell^n\mathscr{F}=\ell^n\mathscr{F}_m/\ell^{m+1}\mathscr{F}_m\) for \(m\geqslant n\), and \(\operatorname{gr}_\ell\mathscr{F}=\bigoplus \operatorname{gr}_\ell^n\mathscr{F}\). This is a sheaf of modules over the noetherian ring \(\operatorname{gr}_\ell\mathbb{Z}=\mathbb{Z}/\ell[t]\), the graded ring of \(\mathbb{Z}\) for the \(\ell\)-adic filtration. It is a quotient of \(\operatorname{gr}_\ell^0\mathscr{F} \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}/\ell} \mathbb{Z}/\ell[t]\), hence a constructible sheaf of \(\operatorname{gr}_\ell\mathbb{Z}\)-modules [2], and there exists a finite partition of \(X\) into locally closed subsets \(X_i\) such that \(\operatorname{gr}_\ell \mathscr{F}|X_i\) are locally constant. Each of the sheaves \(\operatorname{gr}_\ell^n\mathscr{F}|X_i\) is then locally constant, as are the \(\mathscr{F}_m|X_i\), which are successive extensions of them.

If \(\mathscr{F}\) and \(\mathscr{G}\) are two \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaves on \(X\), we set \(\hom(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G}) = \varprojlim(\mathscr{F}_n,\mathscr{G}_n)\); this is a \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-module. Since \(\hom(\mathscr{F}_n,\mathscr{G}_n) = \hom(\mathscr{F}_m,\mathscr{G}_n)\) for \(m\geqslant n\), we again have
\[ \hom(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G}) = \varprojlim_n \varinjlim_m \hom(\mathscr{F}_m,\mathscr{G}_n) \text{,} \]

so that the functor \(\mathscr{F}\mapsto \text{``}\varprojlim\text{''}\mathscr{F}_n\) is fully faithful, from the category of \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaves into that of pro-sheaves on \(X\) (\(=\) pro-objects of the category of sheaves on \(X\)). We shall use it to identify the \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaves with certain pro-sheaves (those such that each \(\mathscr{F}_n=\mathscr{F}/\ell^{n+1}\mathscr{F}\) is a sheaf, and such that \(\mathscr{F}\xrightarrow{\sim} \text{``}\varprojlim\text{''}\mathscr{F}_n\)). One checks easily that if \(\mathscr{F}+\text{``}\varprojlim\text{''}\mathscr{F}_n\), with \(\mathscr{F}_n\) a constructible sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)-modules, then in order for \(\mathscr{F}\) to be a \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf, it is necessary and sufficient that the projective systems (in \(n\)) \(\mathscr{F}_n/\ell^{k+1}\mathscr{F}_n\) be essentially constant: the projective system of the \(\mathscr{F}_k'=\varprojlim_n\mathscr{F}_n/\ell^{k+1}\mathscr{F}_n\) then satisfies the conditions of (2.1), and \(\mathscr{F}=\text{``}\varprojlim\text{''}\mathscr{F}_k'\).

In what follows, we abandon the notation \(\mathscr{F}_n\) of (2.1); if \(\mathscr{F}\) is a \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf, the sheaf \(\mathscr{F}_n\) of (2.1) will be denoted \(\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1}\).

In the abelian category of pro-sheaves, the subcategory of \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaves is stable under kernel, cokernel, and extension. This is clear for cokernels. For kernels, if \(f:\mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{G}\) is a morphism of \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaves, one deduces easily from (2.4, 2.5) and from Artin-Rees that the projective system of the \(\ker(f:\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{G}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n)\) satisfies the criterion given in (2.6) above. There even exists an integer \(r\) such that for all \(n\)

\[ \ker(f)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n = \ker(f:\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+r}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{G}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+r})\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n \text{.} \]
The case of extensions is left to the reader.

A \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) is torsion-free if \(\ker(\ell:\mathscr{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{F}) = 0\). Each \(\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\) is then flat over \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\) (i.e. with fibres free \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)-modules of finite type). One deduces from (2.4, 2.5) that for every \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) there exists an integer \(n\) such that \(\mathscr{F}/\ker(\ell^n)\) is torsion-free.

The abelian category of \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaves on \(X\) is the quotient of that of \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaves by the subcategory of torsion \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaves. In equivalent terms, its objects are the \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaves and, denoting by \(\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Z}_\ell\) the \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\), viewed as an object of the category of \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaves, we have
\[ \hom(\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Q}_\ell,\mathscr{G}\otimes\mathbb{Q}_\ell) = \hom(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_\ell}\mathbb{Q}_\ell \text{.} \]

The fibre of a \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Q}_\ell\) at a geometric point \(x\) of \(X\) is the finite-dimensional \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-vector space \(\mathscr{F}_x\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_\ell}\mathbb{Q}_\ell\).

Let \(X\) be a separated scheme of finite type over an algebraically closed field \(k\), and \(\mathscr{F}\) a constructible \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaf on \(X\). Let \(\mathscr{F}'\) be a constructible \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf such that \(\mathscr{F}\sim \mathscr{F}'\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_\ell}\mathbb{Q}_\ell\). We shall see in (4.11) that
\[ \left(\varprojlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(X,\mathscr{F}'\otimes \mathbb{Z}/\ell^n)\right)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_\ell}\mathbb{Q}_\ell \]

is a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-vector space. It depends only on \(\mathscr{F}'\), and is denoted \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(X,\mathscr{F})\). The proof does not use that \(\ell\) is prime to the characteristic, but only this case is of interest to us.

In this exposé, all the important computations will be carried out at the level of \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)-sheaves, the passage to \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaves being made only at the very last stage. In practice, however, it is often convenient to work systematically with \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaves. In Exposés V and VI of [21], Jouenolou gives the formalism that makes this possible. One of the essential results (VI 2.2) is that if \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) is a separated morphism of finite type of noetherian schemes, and \(\mathscr{F}\) a \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf on \(Y\), then, for each \(q\), the pro-sheaf \(\text{``}\varprojlim\text{''}\mathsf{R}^q f_! (\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n)\) is a \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf on \(Y\). He even proves a stronger regularity property (à la Artin-Rees) for the projective system of the \(\mathsf{R}^q f_!(\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n)\).

Jouanolou even works in a more general framework, encompassing the very useful case of \(E_\lambda\)-sheaves, for \(E_\lambda\) a finite extension of \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\). They are defined as the \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaves were, with \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\) replaced by \(E_\lambda\), \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\) by the ring \(\mathscr{O}_\lambda\) of the valuation \(\lambda\), and \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\) by \(\mathscr{O}_\lambda/\pi^n\), for \(\pi\) a uniformizer. It would amount to the same thing to define an \(E_\lambda\)-sheaf as a \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\), equipped with a homomorphism \(E_\lambda\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\operatorname{End}(\mathscr{F})\).
3 Trace formula and \(L\)-functions
We use the notation of §1, and \(\ell\) is a prime number \(\ne p\).

Let \(X_0\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) (\(q=p^f\)) and \(\mathscr{F}_0\) a constructible \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaf on \(X_0\). Grothendieck's cohomological interpretation of \(L\)-functions is the following theorem:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.1

\(L(X_0,\mathscr{F}_0) = \prod_i \det\left(1-F^* t^f, \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\right)^{(-1)^{i+1}}\).
It is obtained as a consequence of the trace formula:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.2

For every integer \(n\), \(\sum_{x\in X^{F^n}} \operatorname{tr}\left({F^n}^*,\mathscr{F}_x\right) = \sum_i (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}\left({F^n}^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\right)\).

Let us briefly recall the classical method for deducing (3.1) from (3.2). Set \(T=t^f\); the two sides are formal power series in \(T\), with constant term \(1\). Since \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\) is of characteristic \(0\), it suffices to prove that the logarithmic derivatives \(T\frac{d}{dT}\log\) of the two sides are equal.
To compute these logarithmic derivatives, we shall use the formula
\[ T \frac{d}{dT}\log\det(1-f T)^{-1} = \sum_{n>0} \operatorname{tr}(f^n) T^n \text{,} \]
whose proof (in a slightly more general setting) is recalled below. On the left-hand side, one finds

\begin{align*} T\frac{d}{dT}\log L(X_0,\mathscr{F}_0) &= \sum_{x\in |X_0|} \sum_n [k(x):\mathbb{F}_q] \operatorname{tr}\left(F_x^n,\mathscr{F}\right) T^{n\cdot[k(x):\mathbb{F}_q]} \\ &= \sum_{n>0} T^n \sum_{x\in X^{F^n}} \operatorname{tr}\left({F^n}^*,\mathscr{F}_x\right) \end{align*}
and on the right-hand side
\[ \sum_{n>0} T^n \sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}\left({F^n}^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\right) \text{ ; } \]
one compares term by term.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.3

Let \(A\) be a commutative ring, \(M\) a projective \(A\)-module of finite type, and \(f\) an endomorphism of \(M\). For every invertible formal power series \(Q\), we set \(\frac{d}{dT}\log Q = Q^{-1}\frac{d}{dT}Q\). We have

\[ \tag{3.3.1} T\frac{d}{dT}\log\det(1-f T)^{-1} = \sum_{n>0} \operatorname{tr}(f^n) T^n \text{.} \]

Let \(M'\) be an \(A\)-module such that \(M\oplus M'\) is free of finite rank. Replacing \((M,f)\) by \((M\oplus M',f\oplus 0)\) does not change the two sides of (3.3), and reduces us to the case where \(M\) is free. For \(M=A^d\), (3.3.1) is an algebraic identity in the coefficients \(f_i^j\) of \(f\). By the principle of extension of algebraic identities, it suffices to verify it for \(A\) an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(0\). Since the two sides are additive in \(M\) in an extension \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} M''\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\), it even suffices to treat only the case where \(M\) is of rank \(1\). If \(f\) is multiplication by \(a\), (3.3.1) then reduces to the formula
\[ T\frac{d}{dT}\log\left((1-a T)^{-1}\right) = \sum_{n>0} a^n T^n \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.4

Let \(n\) be an integer, and \(f^{(n)}\) the endomorphism \((x_1,\dotsc,x_n)\mapsto \left(f(x_n),x_1,\dotsc,x_{n-1}\right)\) of \(M^n\). We have

\[ \tag{3.4.1} \det(1-f T^n) = \det(1-f^{(n)} T) \text{.} \]
Proceeding as in (3.3), we reduce to assuming that \(A\) is of characteristic \(0\). It then suffices to verify that the logarithmic derivatives \(-T\frac{d}{dT}\log\) of the two sides are equal.

\begin{align*} -T\frac{d}{dT}\log\det(1-f T^n) &= - n T^n \frac{d}{dT^n} \log\det(1-f T^n) = n \sum_{m>0} \operatorname{tr}(f^m) T^{n m} \text{,} \\ -T \frac{d}{dT}\log\det\left(1-f^{(n)} T\right) &= \sum_{m>0} \operatorname{tr}\left(f^{(n) m}\right) T^m \text{,} \end{align*}
and one observes that
\begin{align*} \operatorname{tr}(f^{(n) m}) &= 0 \qquad \text{if } n\nmid m \\ \operatorname{tr}(f^{(n) n m}) &= n \operatorname{tr}(f^m) \text{.} \end{align*}
3.5 Remark

For \(A=\mathbb{Q}_\ell\), (3.4.1) is the special case \(X_0=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})\) of (3.1). Using this identity, it is easy to verify directly that the right-hand side of (3.1) is independent of \(q\), and of the structure morphism \(X_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{F}_q)\).
3.6 Remark

If \(j:X_0\hookrightarrow \overline{X}_0\) is a compactification of \(X_0\), one has \(L(X_0,\mathscr{F}_0) = L(\overline{X}_0, j_!\mathscr{F}_0)\) and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\overline{X},j_!\mathscr{F})\). This reduces (3.1) to the proper case, and explains the use of cohomology with proper supports. For \(X\) proper, (3.2) has the form of a Lefschetz trace formula. One will note that the local terms \(\operatorname{tr}(F^{n *},\mathscr{F}_x)\) (\(x\in X^{F^n}\)) depend only on the fibre of \(\mathscr{F}\) at \(x\), and are not affected by multiplicity. For \(X\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) smooth, this corresponds to the fact that the graph of \(F\) is transverse to the diagonal (since \(d F = 0\)).
3.7 Remark

If one accepts the formalism of \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaves (cf. 2.11; one must have available the Leray spectral sequence and the base change theorem for the higher direct images \(\mathsf{R}^q f_!\)), it is easy to reduce the proof of (3.1, 3.2) to the case where \(X_0\) is a smooth curve and \(\mathscr{F}_0\) is smooth. This is clearly explained in [22] (for 3.1; 3.2 is treated in the same way).
We have two methods for proving (3.2).
Lefschetz-Verdier

If \(X_0\) is proper (cf. 3.6), the general Lefschetz-Verdier trace formula allows one to express the right-hand side of (3.2) as a sum of local terms, one for each point of \(X^{F^n}\). In the original version of [21], this formula was proved only modulo resolution of singularities. The reader will find an unconditional proof in the definitive version. In the case of curves, to which one can reduce (3.7), the ingredients of the proof were moreover all available.
To deduce (3.2) from the Lefschetz-Verdier formula, one must be able to compute its local terms. For a curve and the Frobenius endomorphism, this had been done by Artin and Verdier [40].
Nielson-Wecken
A method inspired by the work of Nielsen and Wecken allows one to reduce (3.2) to a special case proved by Weil; this is what will be explained in the following sections.
4 Reduction to theorems in \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)-cohomology

We shall prove (3.2) by passage to the limit from an analogous theorem in \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)-cohomology. Its statement presents the following difficulty. Let \(X_0\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and \(\mathscr{F}_0\) a flat constructible sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)-modules. Its fibres are free \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)-modules of finite type, and the left-hand side of (3.2) therefore makes sense (it is an element of \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)). On the other hand, the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{F})\) will in general not be free, so that the right-hand side is not defined. Circumventing this difficulty is one of the essential uses made by Grothendieck of the theory of derived categories.

For the definition of the derived category \(\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\) of an abelian category \(\mathscr{A}\), and that of the subcategories \(\mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A})\), \(\mathsf{D}^-(\mathscr{A})\), \(\mathsf{D}^b(\mathscr{A})\), I refer to Verdier's text in this volume. For \(\Lambda\) a ring, one writes \(\mathsf{D}(\Lambda)\) instead of \(\mathsf{D}(\text{category of left } \Lambda \text{-modules})\); for \(X\) a site, one writes \(\mathsf{D}(X,\Lambda)\) instead of \(\mathsf{D}(\)category of sheaves of left \(\Lambda\)-modules\()\). Likewise for \(\mathsf{D}^-\), etc…

The symbol \(\mathsf{R}\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L}\)) indicates a right (resp. left) derived functor. For example, \(\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}\) indicates the derived functor of the tensor product: for \(K\) in \(\mathsf{D}^-(\Lambda^\circ)\) and \(L\) in \(\mathsf{D}^-(\Lambda)\) (\(\Lambda^\circ\) the ring opposite to \(\Lambda\)), \(K\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} L\) is computed as follows: one takes quasi-isomorphisms \(K'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K\), \(L'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} L\), with \(K'\) and \(L\) bounded above and one of them with flat components, and the simple complex \(s(K'\otimes_\Lambda L)\) associated with the double complex \(K'\otimes_\Lambda L'\).

Even to treat the single case of \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\)-cohomology, we shall need the theory of traces of endomorphisms of modules over rings not necessarily commutative (finite group algebras \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n[G]\)). These traces were introduced by Stallings and Hattori [3].

Let \(\Lambda\) be a ring (with unit, but not necessarily commutative). We denote by \(\Lambda^\natural\) the quotient of the additive group of \(\Lambda\) by the subgroup generated by the commutators \(a b - b a\). If \(f\) is an endomorphism of the free left \(\Lambda\)-module \(\Lambda^n\), with matrix \(f_i^j\), we denote by \(\operatorname{tr}(f)\) the image of \(\sum f_i^f\) in \(\Lambda^\natural\). If \(f\) and \(g\) are two homomorphisms \(f:\Lambda^n \leftrightarrows \Lambda^m : g\), one checks immediately that \(\operatorname{tr}(f g) = \operatorname{tr}(g f)\).

Let \(f\) be an endomorphism of a projective \(\Lambda\)-module of finite type \(P\). Let us write \(P\) as a direct factor of a free module \(\Lambda^n\): this means choosing a module \(P'\), and an isomorphism \(\alpha:P\oplus P'\xrightarrow{\sim} \Lambda^n\), or equivalently choosing a homomorphism \(a:P\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \Lambda^n\), and a retraction \(b:\Lambda^n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} P\) (take \(P=\ker(b)\)). Let \(f'=\alpha(f\oplus 0)\alpha^{-1} =af b\). We set \(\operatorname{tr}(f) = \operatorname{tr}(f')\). This element of \(\Lambda^\natural\) depends only on \(f\): if another choice \(c:P\leftrightarrows \Lambda^m:d\) is made, one has \(a=a(dc)(ba)\), whence
\[ \operatorname{tr}(a f b) = \operatorname{tr}(adcbafb) = \operatorname{tr}(cbafbad) = \operatorname{tr}(cfd) \text{.} \]

If \(f\) is an endomorphism of a \(\mathbb{Z}/2\)-graded projective \(\Lambda\)-module of finite type, with components \(f_i^j:P^j\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} P^i\), we set
\[ \operatorname{tr}(f) = \operatorname{tr}(f_0^0) - \operatorname{tr}(f_1^1) \text{.} \]

If there is a risk of ambiguity, we shall write instead \(\operatorname{tr}(f;P)\). If the homomorphisms \(f:P\leftrightarrows Q:g\) are homogeneous, one checks immediately, by reduction to the free case, that
\[ \tag{4.2.1} \operatorname{tr}(f g) = \operatorname{tr}\left((-1)^{\deg f \deg g} g f\right) \text{.} \]

If \(f\) is an endomorphism of a \(\mathbb{Z}/2\)-graded filtered \(\Lambda\)-module \((P,F)\), with finite filtration, compatible with the grading, and if the \(\operatorname{gr}_F^i(P)\) are projective of finite type, then \(P\) is projective of finite type, and
\[ \tag{4.2.2} \operatorname{tr}(f;P) = \sum \operatorname{tr}\left(f; \operatorname{gr}_F^i(P) \right) \]
(split the filtration to reduce to the case of a direct sum).

A \(\mathbb{Z}\)-graded module will be regarded as \(\mathbb{Z}/2\)-graded by the parity of the degree. In particular, if \(f\) is an endomorphism of a bounded complex of projective \(\Lambda\)-modules of finite type, we set
\[ \tag{4.3.1} \operatorname{tr}(f) = \sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}(f^i) \text{.} \]
By (4.2.1), if \(f\) is homotopic to zero, \(\operatorname{tr}(f) = 0\):
\[ \tag{4.3.2} f = d H + h D \rightarrow \operatorname{tr}(f) = 0 \text{.} \]

Let \(\mathsf{K}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\) be the category whose objects are the bounded complexes of projective \(\Lambda\)-modules of finite type, and whose arrows are the morphisms of complexes taken up to homotopy. The functor \(\mathsf{K}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathsf{D}(\Lambda)\) is fully faithful. We denote by \(\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\) its essential image. The formulas (4.3.1) (4.3.2) allow one to define \(\operatorname{tr}(f)\) for \(f\) an endomorphism of \(K\in\operatorname{Ob} \mathsf{D}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\) (and this trace depends only on the isomorphism class of \((K,f)\)).

Recall that the filtered derived category \(\mathsf{DF}(\mathscr{A})\) of an abelian category \(\mathscr{A}\) is the category obtained from that of complexes of filtered objects of finite filtration of \(\mathscr{A}\) by inverting the filtered quasi-isomorphisms (\(=\) morphisms of filtered complexes inducing a quasi-isomorphism on the associated graded). One has functors “underlying complex”: \(\mathsf{DF}(\mathscr{A})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A}): (K,F)\mapsto K\) and “\(p\)-th component of the graded”: \(\mathsf{DF}(\mathscr{A})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A}): (K,F)\mapsto \operatorname{gr}_F^p(K)\).

Let \(\mathsf{KF}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\) be the category whose objects are the complexes bounded filtered of finite filtration \((K,F)\) with the \(\operatorname{gr}_F^p(K^q)\) projective of finite type, and whose arrows are the morphisms of complexes respecting the filtration, taken up to a homotopy respecting the filtration. The functor \(\mathsf{KF}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathsf{DF}(\Lambda)\) is fully faithful; its essential image \(\mathsf{DF}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\) is almost all zero; if \((K,F)\) is in \(\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\), then \(K\) is in \(\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\).
By (4.2.2), if \(f\) is an endomorphism of \((K,F)\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{DF}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\), we have
\[ \tag{4.4.1} \operatorname{tr}(f,K) = \sum_p \operatorname{tr}(f,\operatorname{gr}_F^p(K)) \text{.} \]

Let \(\Lambda\) be a ring, and \(K\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^-(\Lambda)\). We say that \(K\) is of tor-dimension \(\leqslant r\) if, for every right \(\Lambda\)-module \(N\), the hypertors \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(N\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_\Lambda K)\) vanish for \(i<-r\). It is said to be of finite tor-dimension if this condition holds for some \(r\).
The same terminology is used for a complex of sheaves \(K\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^-(X,\Lambda)\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.5.1

Let \(\Lambda\) be a left noetherian ring, and \(K\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^-(\Lambda)\). For \(K\) to lie in \(\mathsf{DF}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\), it is necessary and sufficient that it be of finite tor-dimension and that the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(K)\) be of finite type.

Replacing \(K\) by an isomorphic complex (in \(\mathsf{D}^-(\Lambda)\)) if necessary, we may assume that \(K\) is bounded above with free components of finite type (cf. 4.7, below). If \(K\) is of tor-dimension \(\leqslant r\), the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(K)\) vanish for \(i<-r\), and \(K^{-r}/\operatorname{im}(d)\) admits the free resolution

\[ (\cdots \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K^{-r-1} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K^{-r}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K^{-r}/\operatorname{im}(d) \text{,} \]

and for every right \(\Lambda\)-module \(N\), \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{-r-k}(N\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_\Lambda K) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{-r-k}(N\otimes_\Lambda K) = \operatorname{Tor}_k(N,K^r/\operatorname{im} d)\) for \(k\geqslant 1\).
By hypothesis, these groups vanish; the module \(K^r/\operatorname{im} d\) is therefore flat of finite presentation, i.e. projective of finite type. The quotient

\[ 0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K^r/\operatorname{im}(d) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K^{r+1} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K^{r+2}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \cdots \]
of \(K\) is quasi-isomorphic to \(K\), and this shows that \(K\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{DF}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\).

blocks.title: Proposition-definition
blocks.html:
Proposition-definition 4.6

Let \(X\) be a noetherian scheme, and \(\Lambda\) a left noetherian ring. We denote by \(\mathsf{D}_\textnormal{ctf}^b(X,\Lambda)\) the subcategory of \(\mathsf{D}^-(X,\Lambda)\) formed by the complexes \(\mathscr{K}\) satisfying the following equivalent conditions:

  1. \(\mathscr{K}\) is isomorphic (in \(\mathsf{D}^-(X,\Lambda)\)) to a bounded complex of sheaves of flat and constructible \(\Lambda\)-modules.

  2. \(\mathscr{K}\) is of finite tor-dimension and the sheaves \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(K)\) are constructible.
Same argument as in (4.5), starting from the following lemma.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.7

If a complex \(\mathscr{K}\) of sheaves of \(\Lambda\)-modules is such that the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\mathscr{K}))\) are constructible, and vanish for \(i\) large, then there exists a quasi-isomorphism \(\mathscr{K}'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{K}\), with \(\mathscr{K}'\) bounded above and having constructible and flat components.

We construct \(\mathscr{K}'\) by propagating from right to left. For an \(m\) such that the \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\mathscr{K})\) (\(i\geqslant m\)) vanish, we take \({\mathscr{K}'}^i = 0\) for \(i\geqslant m\). Suppose now that the \({\mathscr{K}'}^i\) have already been constructed for \(i>n\):
\[ \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r] & \mathscr{K}^{n-1} \ar[r] & \mathscr{K}^n \ar[r] & \mathscr{K}^{n+1} \ar[r] & \cdots \\ & & & \mathscr{K}'^{n+1} \ar[u] \ar[r] & \cdots , } \]

with \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\mathscr{K}')\xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\mathscr{K})\) for \(i>n+1\), and \(\ker(d)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{n+1}(\mathscr{K})\) surjective in degree \(n+1\). Let us define sheaves \(\mathscr{A}\) and \(\mathscr{B}\) by the cartesian diagram
\[ \xymatrix{ \mathscr{K}^n \ar[r] & \mathscr{K}^n/\operatorname{im}(d) \ar[r] & \ker(d) \\ \mathscr{A} \ar[u] \ar[r]^u & \mathscr{B} \ar[u]\ar[r] & \ker(d) \ar[u] . } \]

Then \(\mathscr{B}\) is constructible, \(u\) is surjective, and to advance one step it suffices to construct \(K^n\) flat and constructible and \(v:\mathscr{K}^n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{A}\) such that \(u v\) is surjective. That this is possible is guaranteed by the following lemma.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.8

Let \(v:\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{B}\) be an epimorphism of sheaves of \(\Lambda\)-modules, with \(\mathscr{B}\) constructible. Then there exists \(u:\mathscr{K}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{A}\) with \(\mathscr{K}\) flat and constructible and \(v u\) an epimorphism.

The sheaf \(\mathscr{A}\) is a quotient of a sum of sheaves of the form \(\varphi_! \Lambda\), for \(\varphi:U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) étale. Since \(\mathscr{B}\) is noetherian ([2]), a finite sum of these already maps onto \(\mathscr{B}\), whence the lemma.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.9

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) be a separated morphism of finite type of noetherian schemes. If \(\mathscr{K}\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\textnormal{ctf}^b(X,\Lambda)\), then \(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathscr{K}\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\textnormal{ctf}^b(Y,\Lambda)\).

Recall that if \(j:X\hookrightarrow \overline{X} \xrightarrow{\overline{f}} Y\) is a relative compactification of \(X/Y\), then by definition \(\mathsf{R} f_! = \mathsf{R} \overline{f}_* \circ j_!\), where \(\mathsf{R} \overline{f}_*\) is the derived functor of the functor \(\overline{f}_*\). This formula reduces the proof of (4.9) to the case where \(f\) is proper. For \(f\) proper, \(f_*\) is of finite cohomological dimension; this allows us to define \(\mathsf{R} f_*\) on the whole derived category, and also as a functor
\[ \mathsf{R} f_* : \mathsf{D}^-(X,\Lambda) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}^-(Y,\Lambda) \text{.} \]
By composition, one likewise defines, in general,
\[ \mathsf{R} f_! : \mathsf{D}^-(X,\Lambda) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}^-(Y,\Lambda) \text{.} \]
For every right \(\Lambda\)-module \(N\), one has (proof given below)
\[ \tag{4.9.1} N\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathsf{R} f_! \mathscr{K} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R} f_! (N\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathscr{K}) \text{.} \]
Let us deduce (4.9) from (4.9.1).

1. The spectral sequence

    \[ E_2^{p q} = \mathsf{R}^p f_! \underline{\operatorname{H}}^q(\mathscr{K}) \rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{p+q} \mathsf{R} f_! \mathscr{K} \text{.} \]

    and the finiteness theorem for \(\mathsf{R} f_!\) show that \(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathscr{K}\in \operatorname{Ob} \mathsf{D}^b(X,\Lambda)\) and has constructible cohomology. It remains to prove the finite tor-dimension (4.6).

  2. If \(\mathscr{K}\) is of tor-dimension \(\leqslant -r\), the same holds for \(\mathsf{R} f_! \mathscr{K}\): one has \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(N\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathsf{R} f_! \mathscr{K}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(\mathsf{R} f_!(N\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathscr{K}))\), and, in the above spectral sequence for \(N\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathscr{K}\), the \(E_2^{p q}\) vanish for \(q<r-s\), a fortiori for \(p+q<r\).
Let us prove (4.9.1), remaining at the level of complexes.

1. Using the defining formula \(\mathsf{R} f_! = \mathsf{R} f_*\circ j_!\), we reduce to assuming \(f\) proper.

  2. Represent \(\mathscr{K}\) by a complex bounded above with components acyclic for \(f_*:\mathsf{R}^p f_* \mathscr{K}^q = 0\) for \(p>0\). One then has \(\mathsf{R} f_* K \sim f_* \mathscr{K}\). It is possible to work in this way with complexes bounded above only because \(f_*\) is of finite cohomological dimension.

  3. If \(L\) is a free right \(\Lambda\)-module, one has \(\mathsf{R}^p f_*(L\otimes \mathscr{K}^q) = L\otimes \mathsf{R}^p f_* \mathscr{K}^q\): this is trivial for \(\Lambda\) free of finite type, and the general case follows by passage to the limit. The sheaf \(L\otimes \mathscr{K}^q\) is acyclic for \(f_*\), and \(f_*(L\otimes \mathscr{K}^q) = L\otimes f_* \mathscr{K}^q\).

  4. Let \(N_\bullet\) be a free resolution of \(N\). One has \(N\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathscr{K}\sim s(N_\bullet\otimes \mathscr{K})\) (the simple complex associated with the double complex \(N_\bullet\otimes \mathscr{K}\)). By c),

    \[ \mathsf{R} f_*(N\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathscr{K}) \sim \mathsf{R} f_* (s(N_\bullet\otimes \mathscr{K})) \sim f_*(s(N_\bullet\otimes \mathscr{K})) \sim s(N_\bullet\otimes f_* \mathscr{K}) \sim N\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathsf{R} f_* \mathscr{K} \text{,} \]

    which is the announced formula.

When \(Y\) is the spectrum of a separably closed field, the functor \(\mathsf{R} f_!\) is identified with a functor denoted \(\mathsf{R} \Gamma_c : \mathsf{D}_\text{ctf}^b(X,\Lambda)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.10

With the notations of §1, let \(X_0\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and \(\Lambda\) a noetherian torsion ring, killed by an integer prime to \(p\). Let \(\mathscr{K}_0\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\textnormal{ctf}^b(X_0,\Lambda)\). With the definition (4.3) of traces, one has for every \(N\)

\[ \sum_{x\in X^{F^n}} \operatorname{tr}\left({F^n}^*,\mathscr{K}_x\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left({F^n}^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K})\right) \text{.} \]
In the remainder of this §, we shall deduce 3.2 from 4.10, and prove 2.10.
4.11 Proof of 2.10

Let \(X\) be a separated scheme of finite type over an algebraically closed field \(k\), and let \(\mathscr{G}\) be a \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaf on \(X\). By 2.8, we can write it in the form \(\mathscr{G}=\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Q}_\ell\), with \(\mathscr{F}\) a torsion-free \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf. Set
\[ K_n = \mathsf{R} \Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1})\in\mathsf{D}(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1}) \text{.} \]
By 4.9, one has \(K_n\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1})\), and it follows from (4.9.1) that the natural arrow
\[ \tag{4.11.1} \xymatrix{ K_n\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1}} \mathbb{Z}/\ell^n \ar[r] & K_{n+1} , } \]
is an isomorphism. The problem of defining this arrow is discussed in 4.12.

We can now invoke [21] (p. 31, 1-2 to the end; this passage is independent of the rest of [21]) in order to realize each \(K_n\) by a bounded complex of free \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1}\)-modules of finite type, and the arrows (4.11.1) by isomorphisms of complexes
\[ \xymatrix{ K_n\otimes \mathbb{Z}/\ell^n \ar[r]^-\sim & K_{n-1} . } \]
Let \(K\) be the complex \(\varprojlim K_n\). It is a bounded complex of free \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-modules, and \(K_n\simeq K\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_\ell}\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1}\). One has
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(K) = \varprojlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(K_n) \text{,} \]
(every projective system of finite groups indeed satisfies the Mittag-Leffler condition), and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(K)\) is a \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-module of finite type. One has
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{G}) = \left(\varprojlim \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(K_n) \right)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_\ell} \mathbb{Q}_\ell \text{:} \]
it is a \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-vector space of finite dimension.
4.12 The arrow (4.11.1)

To define the arrow (4.11.1), we cannot proceed as in 4.9, i.e. resolve \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\) by a complex of free \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1}\)-modules, since we want to construct an isomorphism in \(\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n)\). The desired arrow is a special case of the following extension-of-scalars arrow.

(*) Let \(\Lambda\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\Lambda'\) be a homomorphism of noetherian torsion rings. For \(X\) a separated scheme of finite type over an algebraically closed field \(k\), and \(\mathscr{K}\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{ctf}(X,\Lambda)\), one has an isomorphism
\[ \xymatrix{ \mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K})\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_\Lambda \Lambda' \ar[r]^-\sim & \mathsf{R} \Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_\Lambda \Lambda') . } \]
More general arrows are constructed in [2]. The method is as follows:

1. The definition of \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c\) and the formula \(j_!(\mathscr{K}\otimes_\Lambda\Lambda') = (j_! \mathscr{K})\otimes_\Lambda\Lambda'\) for an open immersion reduce us to the case where \(X\) is proper.

  2. For \(X\) proper, it is a matter of replacing \(\mathscr{K}\) by a bounded complex whose components are acyclic for the functor \(\Gamma\), and whose stalk at every geometric point (or only at every closed point) is homotopic to a complex of flat \(\Lambda\)-modules. For such a complex, one has \(\Gamma(X,\mathscr{K})\sim \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,\mathscr{K})\) and \(K\otimes_\Lambda\Lambda'\sim \mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_\Lambda\Lambda'\); the arrow (4.11.1) is defined as the composition

    \[ \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,\mathscr{K})\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_\Lambda \Lambda' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \Gamma(X,\mathscr{K})\otimes_\Lambda\Lambda' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \Gamma(X,\mathscr{K}\otimes_\Lambda\Lambda') \xleftarrow{\sim} \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}_\Lambda\Lambda') \text{.} \]

  3. It remains to show that it is possible to replace \(\mathscr{K}\) by a complex of the desired type [2]. One first replaces \(\mathscr{K}\) by a bounded complex with flat components (4.6), then takes a truncated canonical flasque resolution of it (this does not change the homotopy type of the stalk complexes, and one truncates far enough that the acyclicity condition for \(\Gamma\) is satisfied (i.e. beyond the cohomological dimension of \(\Gamma\))).
4.13 Proof of (3.2)
To simplify the notations, we shall treat only the case \(n=1\) of (3.2). The general case is deduced from it by replacing \(F\) by \(F^n\) below.

So let \(X_0\) be separated of finite type over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and \(\mathscr{G}_0\) a \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell\)-sheaf on \(X_0\). One has \(\mathscr{G}_0=\mathscr{F}_0\otimes\mathbb{Q}_\ell\), for a suitable torsion-free \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)-sheaf \(\mathscr{F}_0\). Let \(K_n=\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n)\). The Frobenius morphisms induce morphisms
\[ F^* : K_n\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} K_n \qquad \text{(in } \mathsf{D}_\text{parf}(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1}) \text{),} \]
which are deduced from one another via the isomorphisms (4.11.1).

Let us realize, as in (4.11), the \(K_n\) and the isomorphisms (4.11.1) at the level of complexes. The passage already cited from [21] allows one to realize the morphisms \(F^*\) by endomorphisms of complexes, still denoted \(F^*\), which reduce onto one another. We again denote by \(F^*\) their projective limit, and the endomorphisms deduced from it. Since \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(X,\mathscr{G}) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(K)\otimes\mathbb{Q}_\ell = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(K\otimes\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\), one has (with the sign convention of (?.1)

\[ \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*, \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X,\mathscr{G})\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,K^\bullet\otimes\mathbb{Q}_\ell\right) = \varprojlim_n \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,K_n^\bullet\right) = \varprojlim_n \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1})\right) \text{.} \]
Let us apply (4.10) to \(\mathscr{F}_0\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1}\) (viewed as a complex concentrated in degree \(0\)), for \(\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1}\). One finds that

\begin{align*} \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1})\right) &= \sum_{x\in X^F} \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathscr{F}_x\otimes\mathbb{Z}/\ell^{n+1}\right) \\ &= \sum_{x\in X^F} \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathscr{G}_x\right) \mod \ell^{n+1} \text{,} \end{align*}
and (3.2) then follows by passage to the limit.
5 The Nielsen-Wecken method
In this chapter, we prove two special cases of (4.10). The general case will be considered in the following chapter.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.1

The theorem (4.10) is true for \(X_0\) of dimension \(0\).

In dimension \(0\), the formula (4.10) holds for every correspondence, and not only for the iterates of a Frobenius. It is a special case of the following statement (applied to \(X(\mathbb{F})\), \(K\) and to the \({F^*}^n\)).

(*) Let \(X\) be a finite set, \(F:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\), \(\mathscr{K}\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}(X,\Lambda)\) and \(F^*:F^* \mathscr{K}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{K}\). One has
\[ \sum_{X^F} \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathscr{K}_x\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\Gamma(X,K)\right) \text{.} \]

One has \(\Gamma(X,\mathscr{K})=\bigoplus_{x\in X} \mathscr{K}_x\), and the formula follows from the fact that for every morphism \(u:\bigoplus_{x\in X} \mathscr{K}_x\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \bigoplus_{x\in X} \mathscr{K}_x\), with matrix \(u_x^y\), one has \(\operatorname{tr}(u)=\sum_{x\in X} \operatorname{tr}\left(u_x^x\right)\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.2

Let \(\Lambda\) be a noetherian torsion ring, killed by a power of the prime number \(\ell\ne p\), \(X_0\) a projective, smooth and connected curve over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), \(j:U_0\hookrightarrow X_0\) a dense open of \(X_0\) and \(\mathscr{G}_0\) a locally constant sheaf of projective \(\Lambda\)-modules on \(U_0\). One has

\[ \sum_{x\in U^F} \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathscr{G}_x\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,\mathscr{G})\right) \text{.} \]
More precisely, we shall deduce (5.2) from the

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.3

Let \(X\) be a nonsingular projective curve over an algebraically closed field \(k\), \(f\) an endomorphism of \(X\) with isolated fixed points, and \(v(f)\) the number of fixed points of \(f\), each counted with its multiplicity: \(v(f)\) is the intersection number of the graph of \(f\) with the diagonal of \(X\times X\). Then, for \(\ell\) prime to the characteristic exponent of \(k\), one has

\[ v(f) = \sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}\left(f^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\right) \text{.} \]

This theorem is due to Weil ([41], n\(^\circ\) 43, 66 and 68) and Weil's proof is reproduced in Lang [26] (VI §3 combined with VII §2 th.3). One can also deduce it from the formalism of the cohomology class associated with a cycle ([Cycle] 3.7).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.4

Let \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) be a dense open of \(X\), such that \(f^{-1}(U)=U\). If the fixed points of \(f\) in \(X\setminus U\) are of multiplicity one, then the number \(v_U(f)\) of fixed points of \(f\) in \(U\) (each counted with its multiplicity) is

\[ v_U(f) = \sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}\left(f^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(U,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\right) \text{.} \]

Let \(F\) be the finite set \(X\setminus U\). The exact cohomology sequence defined by the short exact sequence \(0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} j_! \mathbb{Q}_\ell\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{Q}_\ell\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\mathbb{Q}_\ell}_F\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\):

\[ \xymatrix{ \ar[r]^-\partial & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(U,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(F,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \ar[r]^-\partial & } \]
yields, with the sign convention of (3.1).

\[ \operatorname{tr}\left(f^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(U,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(f^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\right) - \operatorname{tr}\left(f^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(F,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\right) = v(f) - \operatorname{tr}(f^*,\mathbb{Q}_\ell^F) \text{.} \]
The trace of \(f^*\) on \(\mathbb{Q}_\ell^F\) is the number \(v_F(f)\) of fixed points of \(f\) in \(F\); the multiplicity-one hypothesis therefore ensures that
\[ \operatorname{tr}\left(f^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(U,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\right) = v_F(f) - v_U(f) \text{,} \]
as promised.
The proof of (5.2) uses several lemmas that we shall now develop, concerning a special case of the non-commutative traces (4.2). For brevity, we shall say projective for projective of finite type.

Let \(\Lambda\) be a ring, and \(H\) a finite group. The map \(\sum a_h \cdot a\mapsto \) class of \(a_e\), from the group algebra \(\Lambda[H]\) to \(\Lambda^\natural\), vanishes on the commutators \(ab-ba\) of \(\Lambda[H]\). It therefore factors through
\[ \varepsilon : \Lambda[H]^\natural \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \Lambda^\natural \text{.} \]
If \(F\) is an endomorphism of a projective \(\Lambda[H]\)-module \(P\), we set
\[ \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda^H(F) = \varepsilon \operatorname{tr}_{\Lambda[H]} (F) \]
where the trace (4.2) appears on the right-hand side. To avoid ambiguities, we shall sometimes write this trace as \(\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda^H(F,P)\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.6

\(\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(F) = |H|\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda^H(F)\).

The formal properties of traces reduce us to treating only the case where \(P=\Lambda[H]\). The endomorphism \(F\) is then right multiplication by an element \(\sum a_h\cdot h\) of \(\Lambda[H]\), and \(\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(F) = |H| a_e\), \(\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda^H(F) = a_e\).

Let \(A\) be a commutative ring and \(\Lambda\) an \(A\)-algebra. Multiplication by an element of \(A\) passes to the quotient to define an \(A\)-module structure on \(A^\natural\). If \(H\) is a finite group, \(P\) a projective \(A[H]\)-module and \(M\) a \(\Lambda[H]\)-module, projective as a \(\Lambda\)-module, it is known that the \(\Lambda\)-module \(P\otimes_A H\), equipped with the diagonal action of \(H\), is a projective \(\Lambda[H]\)-module. Indeed:

1. It suffices to verify it for \(P=A[H]\).

  2. The \(\Lambda\)-module \(P\otimes_A M\), equipped with the action of \(H\) defined by its action on the first factor, is clearly a projective \(\Lambda[H]\)-module; denote it \((P\otimes_A M)'\).

  3. The map \(h\otimes m\mapsto h\otimes h^{-1} m\) induces an isomorphism

    \[ \tag{5.7.1} A[H]\otimes_A M \xrightarrow{\sim} (A[H]\otimes_A M)' \text{.} \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.8

With the preceding notations, if \(u\) is an endomorphism of \(F\) and \(v\) an endomorphism of \(M\), one has

\[ \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda^H(u\otimes v) = \operatorname{tr}_A^H(u)\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(v) \text{.} \]

We reduce to assuming that \(P=A[H]\); the endomorphism \(u\) is then right multiplication \(m_x\) by an element \(x=\sum a_h h\) of \(A[H]\). The isomorphism (5.7.1) transforms \(u\otimes v\) into \(\sum a_h m_h\otimes h^{-1} v\), of trace \(a_e\cdot\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(v)\).
Let \(G\) be a group extension of \(\mathbb{Z}\) by a finite group \(H\)

\[ 1 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} H \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} G \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 1 \text{,} \]

and \(G^+\) the inverse image of \(\mathbb{N}\). Let \(\Lambda\) be a ring, and \(P\) a \(\Lambda[G^+]\)-module, projective as a \(\Lambda[H]\)-module. If \(g\in G^+\), we denote by \(Z_g\) the centralizer of \(g\) in \(H\); multiplication by \(g\) is an endomorphism of \(P\), viewed as a \(\Lambda[Z_g]\)-module. Since \(P\) is \(\Lambda[Z_g]\)-projective, a trace \(\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda^{Z_g}(g)\) is defined. By 5.6, one has
\[ \tag{5.9.1} \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(g) = |Z_g| \cdot \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda^{Z_g}(g) \text{.} \]

Suppose that \(\Lambda\) is an algebra over a commutative ring \(A\). For \(P\) an \(A[G^+]\)-module, projective as an \(A[H]\)-module, and \(M\) a \(\Lambda[G^+]\)-module, projective as a \(\Lambda\)-module, the \(\Lambda[G^+]\)-module \(P\otimes_A M\) (diagonal action of \(G^+\)) is projective as a \(\Lambda[H]\)-module and, by 5.8, for every \(g\in G^+\), one has
\[ \tag{5.9.2} \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda^{Z_g}(g,P\otimes_A M) = \operatorname{tr}_A^{Z_g}(g,P) \cdot \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(g,M) \text{.} \]

Let \(P\) be a \(\Lambda[G^+]\)-module projective as a \(\Lambda[H]\)-module, and \(P_H\) the coinvariants of \(H\) in \(P\). It is a projective \(\Lambda\)-module. The action of \(g\in G^+\) passes to the quotient, and defines an endomorphism of \(P_H\) which depends only on the image of \(g\) in \(\mathbb{N}\). We denote by \(F\) the action of the elements \(g\in G^+\) of image \(1\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.11

\(\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(F,P_H) = \sum_{g\mapsto 1}' \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda^{Z_g}(g,P)\), where \(\sum_{g\mapsto 1}'\) denotes a sum over the \(H\)-conjugacy classes of elements of \(G^+\) of image \(1\) in \(\mathbb{N}\).
After multiplication by \(|H|\), this formula can be verified as follows:

\[ |H|\cdot \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(F,P_H) = \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda\left(\sum_{g\mapsto 1} g,P\right) = \sum_{g\mapsto 1}' \frac{|H|}{|Z_g|}\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(g,P) = \sum_{g\mapsto 1}' |H|\cdot \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda^{Z_g}(g,P) \text{.} \]

Let us choose an element \(g\in G^+\) of image \(1\) in \(\mathbb{N}\), and let \(\sigma\) be the automorphism of \(\Lambda[H]\) induced by the automorphism \(\operatorname{ad} g\) of \(H\). Giving a \(\Lambda[G^+]\)-module amounts to the same thing as giving a \(\Lambda[H]\)–module equipped with a \(\sigma\)-linear endomorphism \(\gamma\): one makes \(g^n h\) act by \(\gamma^n h\). In this language, formula 5.11 takes the form: for \(P\) a projective \(\Lambda[H]\)-module and for \(\gamma\) a \(\sigma\)-linear endomorphism of \(P\), one has
\[ \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(\gamma,P_H) = \sum_h' \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda^{Z_g}(h\gamma,P)\text{,} \]
where \(\sum'\) is a sum over the classes of \(\operatorname{ad}g\)-conjugacy in \(H\) (orbits of \(H\) acting on it via the maps \(x\mapsto h x \operatorname{ad} g(h)^{-1}\)).

In this form, the properties of traces reduce us at once to the case where \(P=\Lambda[H]\). The endomorphism \(Y\) then has the form \(x\mapsto \sigma(x) a\), with \(a=\sum a_h h\) in \(\Lambda[H]\). It suffices to treat the universal case where the \(a_h\) are indeterminates. In this case, \(\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}\langle a_h\rangle_{h\in H}\) (non-commutative polynomials) and \(\Lambda^\natural\) is torsion-free: one obtains 5.11 by the argument at the beginning and division by \(|H|\). One can also compute directly.
Everything said above applies equally well to \(\mathbb{Z}/2\)-graded modules, or to complexes of modules (cf. 4.2, 4.3).

Let us take up again the notations of 5.2, and let \(A=\mathbb{Z}/\ell^n\), with \(n\) large enough that \(\Lambda\) is an \(A\)-algebra. Let \(f:V_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} U_0\) be a finite étale connected covering of \(U_0\), Galois with Galois group \(H\), and such that the sheaf \(f^*\mathscr{G}_0\) is constant. We denote by \(M\) the constant value \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(V_0,f^*\mathscr{G}_0)\); it is a \(\Lambda[H]\)-module, projective as a \(\Lambda\)-module.

The sheaf \(f_* A\) on \(U_0\), equipped with the natural action of \(H\), is a locally free sheaf (of rank one) of \(A[H]\)-modules. The complex \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,f_* A)\) is therefore an object of \(\mathsf{D}_\text{parf}\left(A[H]\right)\). It is equipped with a Frobenius endomorphism \(F^*\).

For the natural action of \(H\) on \(f_* f^*\mathscr{G}_0\), the trace morphism \(f_* f^*\mathscr{G}_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{G}_0\) factors through an isomorphism
\[ \left(f_* f^*\mathscr{G}_0\right)_H \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{G}_0 \text{.} \]
Moreover, one has \(f_* f^*\mathscr{G}_0=f_* A\otimes_A M\) (with diagonal action of \(H\)). The isomorphism
\[ \xymatrix{ \mathscr{G}_0 & (f_* A\otimes_A M)_H = (f_* A\otimes_A M)\otimes_{\Lambda[H]} \Lambda \ar[l]_-\sim} \]
gives, upon deriving (4.12), an isomorphism
\[ \mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,\mathscr{G}) \sim \left(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,f_* A)\otimes_A M\right)\otimes_{\Lambda[H]} \Lambda \text{.} \]

The endomorphism \(F^*\) of the left-hand side is deduced from the endomorphism \(F^*\) of \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,f_* A)\). The complex of \(\Lambda[H]\)-modules \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,f_* A)\), equipped with \(F^*\), can be viewed as a complex of \(\Lambda[G^+]\)-modules, for \(G^+=H\times \mathbb{N}\). Formulas 5.10 and (5.9.2), amplified by 5.11.1, therefore yield
\[ \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,\mathscr{G})\right) = \sum_h' \operatorname{tr}_A^{Z_g}\left(h F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,f_* A)\right)\cdot \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(h,M) \]
where \(\sum'\) is a sum over the conjugacy classes in \(H\). Moreover,
\[ |Z_h|\cdot \operatorname{tr}_A^{Z_h}\left(h F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,f_ A)\right) = \operatorname{tr}_A\left((F h^{-1})^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(V,A)\right) \text{.} \]

This formula remains true for \(A=\mathbb{Z}/\ell^m\), with \(m\) larger and larger. Passing to the limit, one finds that \(\operatorname{tr}_A^{Z_g}\left(h F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,f^* A)\right)\) equals
\[ \frac{1}{|Z_h|} \sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}\left((F h^{-1})^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(V,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\right) \]
(an element of \(\mathbb{Z}_\ell\)), and

\[ \tag{5.12.1} \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,\mathscr{G})\right) = \sum_h' \frac{1}{|Z_h|} \operatorname{tr}\left((F h^{-1})^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(V,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\right)\cdot \operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(h,M) \text{.} \]

It now remains to apply 5.4 (note that if \(\overline{V}\) is the non-singular projective completion of \(V\), the fixed points of \(F h^{-1}\) all have multiplicity one). This can be done without any computation:
1. If \(U^F=\varnothing\), \(\operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,\mathscr{G})\right) = 0\).

Indeed, \(F h^{-1}\) has no fixed point on \(V\); 5.4 shows that \(\sum (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}\left((F h^{-1})^*,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^i(V,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\right)=0\), and one applies (5.12.1).

1. In the general case, let \(j:U'=U\setminus U^F\hookrightarrow U\). The filtration \(j_! j^* \mathscr{G}_0\subset \mathscr{G}_0\) of \(\mathscr{G}_0\) induces a filtration of \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,\mathscr{G})\) with successive quotients \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U',\mathscr{G})\) and \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U^F,\mathscr{G})\). By (4.4.1) and 5.1, one has

    \[ \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,\mathscr{G})\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U',\mathscr{G})\right) + \sum_{x\in U^F} \operatorname{tr}(F^*,\mathscr{G}_x) \text{,} \]

    and, since \({U'}^F=0\), the first term on the right-hand side is \(0\).

pages.title: End of the proof of 4.10

blocks.html: 6 End of the proof of 4.10

Let us prove 4.10, under the additional hypotheses that the ring \(\Lambda\) is annihilated by a power of a prime number \(\ell\ne p\), and that \(n=1\). The general case will follow from it: decompose \(\Lambda\) into its \(\ell\)-primary components (\(\ell\) ranging over the prime numbers), and replace \(\mathbb{F}_q\) by \(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\), \(X_0\) by \(X_0\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}_{q^n}\).
For \(X_0\) separated and of finite type over \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and \(\mathscr{K}_0\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_\text{ctf}(X_0,\Lambda)\), let us set
\[ T'(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = \sum_{x\in X^F} \operatorname{tr}(F^*,\mathscr{K}_x) \]
and
\[ T''(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = \operatorname{tr}(F^*,\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K})) \text{.} \]
We must prove the identity
\[ (1;X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) \qquad T'(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = T''(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) \text{.} \]
We begin by observing that \(T'\) and \(T''\) (generically denoted \(T\)) obey the same formalism:
(A) If \(j:U_0\hookrightarrow X_0\) is an open subset of \(X_0\), with closed complement \(Y_0\), one has
\[ T(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = T(U_0,\mathscr{K}_0|U_0) + T(Y_0,\mathscr{K}_0|Y_0) \text{.} \]

This is clear for \(T'\). For \(T''\), one observes that the filtration \(0\subset j_! j^* \mathscr{K}_0\subset \mathscr{K}_0\) of \(\mathscr{K}_0\) induces a filtration of \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K})\), with successive quotients \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(U,\mathscr{K})\) and \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(Y,\mathscr{K})\), and one invokes (4.4.1) (more precisely stated: \(\mathscr{K}_0\), equipped with the said filtration, defines an object of \(\mathsf{DF}(X,\Lambda)\); by applying \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c\), one deduces an object of \(\mathsf{DF}_\text{parf}(\Lambda)\), whose underlying object is \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K})\), and whose graded object is as stated).
(B) If \(\mathscr{K}_0\) is a bounded complex with constructible and flat components,
\[ T(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = \sum (-1)^i T(X_0,\mathscr{K}^i) \text{.} \]
This is clear for \(T'\); for \(T''\), one applies the above argument to the stupid filtration of \(\mathscr{K}_0\), to obtain
\[ T''(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = \sum T''(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0^i[-i]) = \sum (-1)^i T''(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0^i) \text{.} \]
(C) For \(f:X_0\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y_0\) a morphism, one has
\[ T''(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = T''(Y_0,\mathsf{R} f_! \mathscr{K}_0) \]
and the same identity holds for \(T'\) if the fibres of \(f\) at the rational points of \(Y_0\) satisfy \(\left(1;f^{-1}(y),\mathscr{K}_0|f^{-1}(y)\right)\): one uses that
\[ T'(X_0,\mathscr{K}_0) = \sum_{y\in Y^F} T'\left(f^{-1}(y), \mathscr{K}_0|f^{-1}(y)\right) \]
and
\[ \mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(Y, \mathsf{R} f_! \mathscr{K}) = \mathsf{R}\Gamma_c(X,\mathscr{K}) \text{.} \]
Using this formalism, and 4.7, one reduces the proof of 4.10 to the two special cases 5.1 and 5.2.
